document.title: Afghanistan: Taliban's Mullah Omar's 8/22 Contact with State Department (State 154712)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Mullah Omar Called Washington in 1998, New Documents Show
document.note: [Confidential (NODIS)] Mullah Omar phones State two days after the 20 Aug 1998 missile strikes and speaks with Michael Malinowski, director for Pakistan, Afghanistan and Bangladesh affairs. It appears to be his only direct contact with a U.S. official. He suggests Clinton resign, predicts more attacks, demands proof of bin Laden's involvement in the Africa bombings, and criticizes the U.S. military presence in Saudi Arabia. Malinowski finds him 'in no way threatening'. Excised.

events.description: A supporter of bin Laden approached Malinowski to ask whether he would communicate with a top Taliban leader.

Mullah Omar spoke by open-line telephone with Malinowski, the first known contact between Omar and a US official; Omar said he was open to dialogue, asked for evidence against bin Laden, and warned the US strikes would be counterproductive.
US strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan, the reason for Omar's contact.
Early-morning open-line conference call between Malinowski at home and Taliban HQ in Kandahar; Mullah Omar joined and spoke, with a translator vouching for his voice.
Omar warned that US strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan would be counterproductive and spark more terrorist attacks, and asked for evidence against bin Laden.
Malinowski urged Omar to place bin Laden and other terrorists in custody or expel them from Afghanistan, and cited Pushtunwali.
The State Department cable 154712 reporting the Omar call was sent to Embassy Islamabad and Consulate Peshawar.

key_claims: On 22 Aug 1998 Mullah Omar spoke by open phone line with State Department official Michael Malinowski, the first known contact between Omar and a US official.
Omar said he knew of no evidence that bin Laden planned terrorist acts from Afghan soil and asked for evidence.
Omar repeated bin Laden-style rhetoric, including calls for US forces to leave the Gulf, while remaining controlled and non-threatening.
Omar warned that US strikes in Afghanistan and Sudan would be counterproductive and could spark more terrorist attacks.
The Taliban were open to a secure channel with the US, possibly via the Islamabad embassy, but Omar suggested the US deal with Taliban representatives in Islamabad.
The US argued that Pushtunwali does not justify sheltering bin Laden and urged Omar to expel or detain him.
The State Department assessed that the contact showed Taliban interest in dialogue but was far from the Taliban doing the right thing on bin Laden.
